newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FOCUS-Taiwan dollar, stocks fall after rate hikes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Taiwan dollar, stocks fall after rate hikes.

text.p: In twin muted responses to central bank interest rate hikes, Taiwan's stock market eased mildly in what one analyst called a "courtesy fall" while the local currency continued to tumble on Friday.

The stock index, which has ascended to several eight-year peaks this week, fell 0.64 percent to 10,001.56 points after the central bank raised its rediscount rate and secured loans rate by a quarter of a percentage point each.

The rate hikes had even less of an impact in the foreign exchange market, where the recently depreciating Taiwan dollar dropped to its lowest level against the U.S. dollar since 1988 despite speculative selling of the greenback in early session.
The Taiwan dollar ended at 28.752 to the dollar on Friday in Taipei, compared to its Thursday close of 28.70.

Analysts said the market reactions appeared to lend credence to the widespread belief that the bank's rate-tightening was more symbolic than substantial and predicted the two markets would stay their courses -- a boom for stocks and a slide for the local dollar.

"The two rates that the central bank hiked have mostly symbolic usage, and by raising them the central bank is sending out a message without actually changing any substantial policies," said United Securities analyst Lin Long-hsien.
"You could call today's stock market a courtesy fall after the central bank's move," Lin said.

The central bank said on Thursday it would not intervene in the foreign exchange market, where the Taiwan dollar has plunged more than four percent this week, unless it noticed egregious speculative action.
"The bank will...let market supply and demand determine the Taiwan dollar exchange rates," governor Sheu Yuan-dong said after the bank's quarterly board meeting.
"But if there are abnormal factors intervening in the market it will adopt appropriate measures to maintain the foreign exchange market's stability," he said.
Sheu said the rate hikes aimed to "stabilise the foreign exchange market". But dealers said the greenback's worldwide strength appeared indomitable for now.
"If the U.S. dollar maintains its strength overseas, the Taiwan dollar will soon stand at above T$28 -- probably tomorrow," a dealer said after Friday's close.
The U.S. dollar topped 119 yen for the first time in 11 weeks on Friday and was bobbing just below Monday's more than seven-year peak against the mark.
Analysts maintain that Taiwan's central bank, despite its stabilisation gestures, actually welcomes a depreciation to boost Taiwan's exports, the engine behind its vibrant economy.

And they say just as inevitable as the Taiwan dollar's foundering is the stock market's inexorable bull charge, which has driven the index to within striking distance of the all-time peak of 12,495.34 set in 1990.
"Basically the government wants to cool down the market, but not so much that the bullish streak is ended," United's Lin said.
"Investors' optimism is enough to lift the market past the all-time high by the end of 1997," said Oliver Fang, senior analyst for National Securities.

Fang and other analysts said the government was sending intentionally mixed messages on the stock market, which has risen a whopping 113 percent since March 1996, in an attempt to coax more gradual growth.
Governor Sheu cited a "consensus" that the market may be slightly overheated with its recent torrential turnover, but said the bank had no opinion on whether the index was too high.
Vice President Lien Chan said earlier this week the index above 10,000 was "very healthy".

But cabinet economic planning chief Chiang Pin-kung said on Thursday the stock surge may have been concocted in part by speculators -- and should not necessarily be seen as a reflection of the island's economic strength.
